query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A combined experimental and ab initio simulation approach that separately models electron–phonon coupling and defect scattering in HfNbTaTiZr with controlled oxygen content will predict both lattice and electronic thermal conductivities more accurately, reducing the discrepancy from measured values by approximately 30% compared to conventional single-parameter Debye-based methods.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy ingots with about 1 wt.% oxygen, processed into dense, defect-controlled bulk samples with minimal porosity.
generation.intervention: Integrate ab initio phonon–electron coupling simulations with time-domain thermoreflectance (TDTR) and electrical resistivity measurements to isolate and quantify phononic and electronic heat contributions.
generation.conditions: Test across 100–1200 K in an inert atmosphere to mitigate oxidation, ensuring stable microstructures and uniform oxygen distribution.
generation.structural_mediator: Interstitial oxygen-induced lattice distortions and varying electron scattering pathways in the complex high-entropy matrix affecting phonon/electron transport.
generation.mechanism: By removing simplifying single-Debye assumptions and explicitly incorporating point-defect scattering in multi-principal element environments, the method captures the actual pathways for heat conduction to yield improved predictions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Thermal conductivity estimates within ±20% of experimental values across the tested temperature range, distinctly partitioning lattice and electronic components and outperforming prior simplified estimates.
generation.baseline: Conventional models for this alloy yield total thermal conductivity in the 10–17 W/(K·m) range but do not reliably separate or predict lattice vs. electronic contributions, especially below 300 K.
generation.boundary: Model validity depends on accurate oxygen control and stable phases; scalability beyond ~1 wt.% oxygen or severely multiphase conditions remains unverified.
generation.uncertainty: Potential microstructural evolutions under prolonged high-temperature exposure and inhomogeneous oxygen distributions may affect predictive accuracy.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce multiple HfNbTaTiZr samples with calibrated oxygen contents, measure total and partitioned (TDTR-based and electrical) conductivity at 100–1200 K, and compare with ab initio predictions incorporating phonon–electron scattering mechanisms.
measurements: Electrical resistivity to infer electronic contribution
Lattice component via subtracting electronic from total conductivity
Phase and defect state via microstructural characterization
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If measured conduction data deviate consistently from predicted values by more than ±20% across multiple sample batches and temperatures, the new predictive approach is invalidated.

cited_evidence.text: These alloys thus provide an ideal system to systematically study how the type and number of elements affect the transport properties of equiatomic alloys. Electrical and thermal transport data are reported for all of the alloys for temperatures between 4 and 300 K, and ab initio KKR- CPA calculations are performed to investigate the origin of high residual resistivity (ρR, resistivity at 0 K). The Wiedemann-Franz relationship is used to estimate the phonon and electron contributions to the measured total thermal conductivity. In addition, magnetization data are reported for the five alloys with three or more elements from 4 to 300 K using applied fields between 0 and 4 Tesla.

Figure 3 shows the temperature dependence of the measured κ, and the derived values of κe and κg for NiCoFeCrMn and NiCoFeCrPd. One distinct feature of the concentrated alloys, relative to pure metals, is that in a pure metal the total thermal conductivity is dominated by κe, and κg is usually negligible. However, in concentrated alloys, κg seems to dominate at low temperatures and is comparable with κe at about room temperature. Chemical disorder appears to scatter electrons more effectively than phonons. In addition, in pure metals κ starts decreasing at a few tens of K, while in concentrated alloys κ keeps increasing up to at least 300 K (see Table 3). One major reason is that, due to the large and nearly constant resistivity of these complex alloys, κe almost linearly increases with temperature up to 300 K, which is very different from the behavior in pure metals. The theoretical description of the temperature dependence of κg for disordered alloys has been challenging. However, numerical calculations of κg in equiatomic binary alloys of NiPd and NiPt show a very similar temperature dependence to what is shown in Fig. 3: at low temperature, κg increases rapidly with temperature

Table 3 lists the κ, κe and κg values at 50 and 300 K for the measured alloys. Here we want to emphasize again that the Wiedemann-Franz law is only a coarse approximation; electron-electron interactions, Fermi smearing, and the “vertical” movement in Fermi surfaces may all lead to deviations. Thus for some low-resistivity alloys, application of the Wiedemann-Franz law results in the situation of κe greater than κ, which is nonrealistic. The thermal conductivity of Ni and NiFe has been previously measured over the temperature regime investigated in this study and that of NiCoFeCr has been measured at 300 K and above. Our results on these materials agree well with the literature values. The total thermal conductivity of these concentrated alloys are significantly lower than that for pure metals, similar to some super-alloys, but the main reason of the reduction in κ is the low κe induced by high electrical resistivity.
